```
# Uniform Circular Motion (UCM)
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🎯 Core Concept & Definition

**Uniform Circular Motion** is the motion of an object moving along a **circular path** with **constant speed**.

> ⚠️ KEY DISTINCTION — Speed is constant, but **velocity is NOT constant** because the **direction** of motion keeps changing at every point.

### What this means physically:
| Quantity | Status in UCM |
|----------|--------------|
| Speed | ✅ Constant |
| Velocity | ❌ Changing (direction changes) |
| Acceleration | ✅ Exists (due to change in velocity direction) |
| Kinetic Energy | ✅ Constant |
| Momentum | ❌ Changing |

### Direction of Key Vectors:
```
        v (tangential)
        ↑
        |
← a ────●──────→ Circle
(centripetal,    
towards center)
```

- **Velocity (v)** → Always **tangential** to the circle (perpendicular to radius)
- **Centripetal Acceleration (a)** → Always **towards the center** (centripetal = "center-seeking")
- **v and a are always perpendicular** → That's why speed doesn't change!

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas

### Angular Velocity (ω)
$$\boxed{\omega = \frac{\theta}{t} = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f}$$

- Unit: **rad/s**
- ω tells how fast the angle sweeps

---

### Relationship Between Linear & Angular Velocity
$$\boxed{v = r\omega}$$

- v = linear/tangential speed (m/s)
- r = radius of circular path (m)

---

### Centripetal Acceleration
$$\boxed{a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}}$$

- Direction: **Always towards the center**
- This is a **real acceleration** (causes direction change)

---

### Centripetal Force
$$\boxed{F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r}$$

- **NOT a new force** — it is the **net force directed towards center**
- It can be provided by: Tension, Gravity, Normal force, Friction, etc.

---

### Time Period & Frequency
$$\boxed{T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}} \quad \text{and} \quad \boxed{f = \frac{1}{T}}$$

---

### 🔴 Centrifugal Force (Pseudo Force)
- Only observed in **rotating (non-inertial) frame**
- Equal in magnitude but **opposite in direction** to centripetal force
- **Does NOT exist** in ground (inertial) frame

---

## 3. 🧠 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Finding centripetal acceleration/force
> "A particle moves in a circle of radius 2m with speed 4 m/s. Find centripetal acceleration."
→ Direct formula: $a = v²/r$

---

### Pattern 2: Angle between velocity and acceleration
> "What is the angle between velocity and acceleration in UCM?"
→ **Always 90°** (they are perpendicular)

---

### Pattern 3: Change in velocity over half/quarter revolution
> "A particle completes half revolution. Find change in velocity."

- After half revolution: velocity reverses direction
$$|\Delta v| = |v_f - v_i| = v - (-v) = 2v$$

- After quarter revolution: directions are perpendicular
$$|\Delta v| = \sqrt{v^2 + v^2} = v\sqrt{2}$$

---

### Pattern 4: Work done by centripetal force
> "How much work is done by centripetal force?"
→ **Work = 0** always! (Force ⊥ displacement, cos90° = 0)

---

### Pattern 5: Comparing quantities when r or v changes
> "If speed doubles with same radius, centripetal force becomes?"
→ $F_c \propto v^2$, so F becomes **4 times**

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tip & Analogy

### 🌀 The Stone-in-a-Sling Analogy:
Imagine swinging a stone tied to a string in a circle:
- Your **hand pulling the string** = Centripetal force (towards center)
- The stone always tries to **fly away tangentially** (Newton's 1st law)
- The moment you release → stone flies off **tangentially** (not outward!)

### 🧠 Memory Tricks:

| Formula | Trick |
|---------|-------|
| $v = rω$ | **"Very Relaxed ω"** → v, r, ω |
| $a = v²/r$ | **"A Very²/Rough road"** |
| Work by F_c = 0 | **Force ⊥ velocity → Zero work** |
| ω = 2πf | **"omega equals 2π × frequency"** → think of full circle (2π) per second |

---

## 5. 📝 Example Problem (NEET-Style)

**Question:**
A particle of mass 0.1 kg is moving in a circular path of radius 1 m. If its angular velocity is 2π rad/s, find:
(a) Linear speed
(b) Centripetal acceleration
(c) Centripetal force

---

**Solution:**

**Given:**
- m = 0.1 kg
- r = 1 m
- ω = 2π rad/s

---

**(a) Linear Speed:**
$$v = r\omega = 1 \times 2\pi = 2\pi \approx 6.28 \text{ m/s}$$

---

**(b) Centripetal Acceleration:**
$$a_c = \omega^2 r = (2\pi)^2 \times 1 = 4\pi^2 \approx 39.5 \text{ m/s}^2$$

---

**(c) Centripetal Force:**
$$F_c = ma_c = 0.1 \times 4\pi^2 = 0.4\pi^2 \approx 3.95 \text{ N}$$

*Direction: Towards the center of the circle*

---

## 🔑 Quick Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         UCM — MUST REMEMBER FOR NEET        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ✅ Speed = constant; Velocity = variable    │
│ ✅ v ⊥ a (always 90° between them)         │
│ ✅ v = rω | a = v²/r | F = mv²/r           │
│ ✅ Work by centripetal force = ZERO         │
│ ✅ Centrifugal force = pseudo force only    │
│ ✅ Release → object moves TANGENTIALLY      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

> 📌 **NEET Tip:** Every year, 1–2 questions appear from UCM. Focus on: centripetal force calculations, change in velocity vectors, and work done. These are the highest-yield sub-topics!

# Resolution of Vectors — Class 11, Chapter 4
## Complete NEET Guide

---

## 1. 🎯 Core Concept & Definition

**Resolution of a vector** is the process of splitting a single vector into **two or more component vectors** that together produce the **same effect** as the original vector.

> Think of it as the **reverse of vector addition** — instead of combining vectors, you break one vector into parts.

### Why Do We Resolve Vectors?
> Because **mathematics is easier along straight lines (axes)** than at angles!

---

### 📐 Resolution in a Plane (2D)

Consider a vector **A** making angle **θ** with the positive X-axis:

```
Y
↑
|   /→ A (resultant)
|  /
| / θ
|/________→ X
```

The vector **A** is resolved into:
- **Horizontal Component (Aₓ)** → along X-axis
- **Vertical Component (Aᵧ)** → along Y-axis

These components are **mutually perpendicular** (at 90° to each other).

---

## 2. 🔑 Key Formulas

### Primary Resolution Formulas:

| Component | Formula | Direction |
|-----------|---------|-----------|
| X-component | **Aₓ = A cos θ** | Along X-axis |
| Y-component | **Aᵧ = A sin θ** | Along Y-axis |

Where:
- **A** = magnitude of original vector
- **θ** = angle with positive X-axis

### In Unit Vector Notation:
$$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}$$
$$\vec{A} = A\cos\theta\,\hat{i} + A\sin\theta\,\hat{j}$$

---

### Reverse Process — Reconstructing from Components:

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| **Magnitude** | $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ |
| **Direction** | $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{A_y}{A_x}\right)$ |

---

### ⚡ Important Angle Table (Memorize!):

| θ | cos θ (→ Aₓ) | sin θ (↑ Aᵧ) |
|---|--------------|--------------|
| 0° | 1 | 0 |
| 30° | √3/2 | 1/2 |
| 45° | 1/√2 | 1/√2 |
| 60° | 1/2 | √3/2 |
| 90° | 0 | 1 |

---

### Resolution in 3D:
$$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$$
$$A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}$$

---

## 3. 📋 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Direct Component Finding
> *"A force of 20 N acts at 60° to the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components."*
- Straightforward: use Aₓ = A cos θ, Aᵧ = A sin θ

---

### Pattern 2: Vector Addition Using Resolution
> *"Two vectors of magnitude 3 and 4 act at 90° to each other. Find the resultant."*
- Resolve each → add components → reconstruct magnitude

---

### Pattern 3: Inclined Plane (Most Common in NEET! ⭐)
> *"A block on a 30° incline... find component of weight along and perpendicular to surface."*

```
       /|
      / |
     /  | mg (downward)
    /θ  |
   /    |
  /_____|
```

- **Along incline** (causes sliding) = **mg sin θ**
- **Perpendicular to incline** (causes normal force) = **mg cos θ**

> 🔴 **NEET Trap:** Many students confuse which is sin and which is cos on inclined planes!
> **Rule:** The component *opposing the steeper direction* uses **sin θ**

---

### Pattern 4: Projectile Motion
> The entire concept of projectile motion is based on resolution!
- **Horizontal:** uₓ = u cos θ (constant, no acceleration)
- **Vertical:** uᵧ = u sin θ (affected by gravity)

---

### Pattern 5: Equilibrium Problems
> *"Three concurrent forces are in equilibrium. Find the unknown force."*
- Sum of X-components = 0
- Sum of Y-components = 0

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tips & Analogies

### 🎭 The "Shadow Analogy":
> Imagine shining a **torch horizontally** on a vector arrow — the **shadow on the wall = vertical component (sin θ)**. Shine the torch **vertically** — the **shadow on the floor = horizontal component (cos θ)**.

---

### 🎵 The Golden Rule to Never Forget:
> **"cos θ goes with the CLOSER axis"**
> If θ is measured from X-axis → X-component uses **cos θ**
> If θ is measured from Y-axis → Y-component uses **cos θ**

---

### 🧠 NEET Shortcut for Inclined Planes:
> Draw the incline. The weight mg goes straight down.
> **"The angle at TOP of the triangle = same as incline angle θ"**
> - mg **sin θ** → **parallel** to slope (along the surface)
> - mg **cos θ** → **perpendicular** to slope (into the surface)

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem (NEET Style)

### Problem:
> A vector **F** = 10 N acts at an angle of 30° above the negative X-axis (in the second quadrant). Find its X and Y components and write it in unit vector notation.

---

### Solution:

**Step 1: Identify the angle properly**

The vector is in the **2nd quadrant**, making 30° with the negative X-axis.
∴ Angle from positive X-axis = **180° - 30° = 150°**

---

**Step 2: Apply resolution formulas**

$$F_x = F\cos 150° = 10 \times \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -5\sqrt{3} \text{ N}$$

$$F_y = F\sin 150° = 10 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = +5 \text{ N}$$

---

**Step 3: Unit vector notation**

$$\boxed{\vec{F} = -5\sqrt{3}\,\hat{i} + 5\,\hat{j} \text{ N}}$$

---

**Step 4: Verify magnitude**

$$F = \sqrt{(-5\sqrt{3})^2 + (5)^2} = \sqrt{75 + 25} = \sqrt{100} = 10 \text{ N ✓}$$

---

**Step 5: Verify direction**

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{|F_y|}{|F_x|} = \frac{5}{5\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow \alpha = 30° \text{ from negative X-axis ✓}$$

---

## 🔴 NEET Common Mistakes to Avoid:

| ❌ Mistake | ✅ Correct Approach |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Using sin for horizontal when angle is from X-axis | Horizontal = **cos θ** when θ from X-axis |
| Forgetting negative signs in 2nd/3rd quadrant | Always check which quadrant! |
| Confusing incline components | Along slope = mg **sin θ**, Normal = mg **cos θ** |
| Not verifying with magnitude formula | Always check: √(Aₓ² + Aᵧ²) = A |

---
```

# Equality of Vectors — Class 11, Chapter 4 | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

> **Two vectors are said to be equal if and only if they have the SAME magnitude AND the SAME direction.**

This seems simple, but students often confuse it — **both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.**

### What Makes Two Vectors Equal?

| Condition | Requirement |
|-----------|-------------|
| Magnitude | Must be **identical** (same numerical value + same unit) |
| Direction | Must be **exactly the same** (same angle, same sense) |

### Critical Point — Position Does NOT Matter!
A vector is a **free vector** — it can be translated (shifted) anywhere in space **without changing its value**, as long as magnitude and direction are preserved.

```
→A = ———→         →B = ———→ (shifted to another location)
     
Both are EQUAL because same length, same direction
```

This means a vector has **no fixed point of application** in the context of equality.

---

## 2. 📐 Key Facts & Mathematical Representation

### Formal Definition:
If **→A = →B**, then:
- |**→A**| = |**→B**| → **(magnitudes are equal)**
- **â = b̂** → **(unit vectors/directions are equal)**

### In Component Form:
Two vectors are equal **if and only if ALL corresponding components are equal:**

$$\vec{A} = \vec{B} \implies A_x = B_x, \quad A_y = B_y, \quad A_z = B_z$$

> This is the **most important and testable** form for NEET!

### What is NOT sufficient for equality:

| Situation | Equal? | Reason |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| Same magnitude, opposite directions | ❌ No | **→A** and **-→A** are NOT equal |
| Same direction, different magnitudes | ❌ No | 5 m/s ≠ 10 m/s even if same direction |
| Same magnitude, perpendicular directions | ❌ No | Direction mismatch |
| Both conditions met, different positions | ✅ Yes | Position is irrelevant |

---

## 3. 🎯 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Component-based equality
> *"If vector →A = 3î + 4ĵ and →B = aî + bĵ, and →A = →B, find a and b"*

**Approach:** Simply equate components → a = 3, b = 4

---

### Pattern 2: Conceptual trap question
> *"A vector →A is displaced parallel to itself to a new position. The new vector is:"*
> - (a) Different from →A
> - (b) Equal to →A ✅
> - (c) Negative of →A
> - (d) Cannot be determined

**Answer: (b)** — Parallel displacement preserves both magnitude and direction.

---

### Pattern 3: Negative vector confusion
> *"Which of the following vectors is NOT equal to →A = 2î + 3ĵ?"*
> - (a) 2î + 3ĵ (at origin)
> - (b) 2î + 3ĵ (at point P)
> - (c) -2î - 3ĵ ← **This one** ❌
> - (d) 2î + 3ĵ (at point Q)

**Trick:** Option (c) is the **negative** of →A, not equal to it.

---

### Pattern 4: Resultant and equality
> *"→A + →B = →A. What can you say about →B?"*

**Answer:** →B must be a **null/zero vector** (→0)
Because: →A + →0 = →A ✅

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tip & Analogy

### The "Twin Brothers Analogy":
> Think of two vectors like twin brothers — they are truly "equal" only if they are **identical in every way**: same height (magnitude) AND facing the same direction. Just because they look the same height but face opposite directions doesn't make them equal — that would make one the "negative" of the other!

---

### Quick Memory Formula:
```
EQUAL VECTORS = Same MAGNITUDE + Same DIRECTION
                     (M)              (D)

Forget either M or D → NOT equal!
```

### Also Remember:
- **Equal vectors** → same magnitude, same direction
- **Negative vectors** → same magnitude, **opposite** direction
- **Null vector** → magnitude = 0, direction undefined

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem with Solution

### Problem:
> Two vectors are given as:
> **→P** = 5î + 12ĵ and **→Q** = 5î + 12ĵ (but →Q is positioned at point (3, 4))
>
> **(a)** Are →P and →Q equal?
> **(b)** What is |→P| and |→Q|?
> **(c)** If →R = 5î - 12ĵ, is →R equal to →P?

---

### Solution:

**(a) Checking equality of →P and →Q:**

Step 1 — Compare components:
- î components: 5 = 5 ✅
- ĵ components: 12 = 12 ✅

Step 2 — Position check:
- Position does NOT affect vector equality

**∴ →P = →Q ✅ (They ARE equal)**

---

**(b) Finding magnitudes:**

$$|\vec{P}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = \boxed{13 \text{ units}}$$

$$|\vec{Q}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = \boxed{13 \text{ units}}$$

*(As expected — equal vectors have equal magnitudes)*

---

**(c) Is →R = →P?**

- →P = 5î + 12ĵ
- →R = 5î **- 12**ĵ

Step 1 — Compare î: 5 = 5 ✅
Step 2 — Compare ĵ: **12 ≠ -12** ❌

**∴ →P ≠ →R**

In fact, |→R| = 13 (same magnitude), **BUT** direction is different.
→R is obtained by reflecting →P across the x-axis.

> 🔑 Key takeaway: **Same magnitude ALONE is not enough for equality!**

---

## 📦 NEET Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         EQUALITY OF VECTORS — NEET FACTS     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ✅ Equal vectors: |A|=|B| AND direction same │
│ ✅ Position/location: DOESN'T matter         │
│ ✅ Component form: Ax=Bx, Ay=By, Az=Bz       │
│ ❌ Same magnitude ≠ necessarily equal        │
│ ❌ Opposite directions = Negative vector     │
│ ❌ Parallel shift changes NOTHING            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

> 💬 **Pro NEET Tip:** Questions on vector equality often appear **embedded inside larger problems** (like relative velocity or projectile motion). Always verify BOTH magnitude and direction before declaring two vectors equal. The most common trap is choosing vectors with equal magnitudes but ignoring direction! 🎯

# 🎯 Projectile Motion — Complete NEET Guide
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

> **A projectile is any object thrown into the air that moves under the influence of gravity alone (no air resistance).**

When you throw a ball at an angle, it follows a **curved path called a trajectory**. This motion has **TWO independent components:**

```
📌 KEY INSIGHT: Horizontal and Vertical motions are COMPLETELY INDEPENDENT of each other
```

| Component | Direction | Acceleration | Type of Motion |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| **Horizontal (x)** | Along ground | **Zero** (no force) | Uniform (constant velocity) |
| **Vertical (y)** | Up/Down | **g = 10 m/s²** (downward) | Uniformly accelerated |

### 🔹 How it's launched:
If a projectile is launched with velocity **u** at angle **θ** with horizontal:

```
        uᵧ = u sinθ (vertical component)
       ↑  ↗
       | /  
       |/ θ
       ────────→ uₓ = u cosθ (horizontal component)
```

- **Horizontal velocity** → `uₓ = u cosθ` *(remains constant throughout)*
- **Vertical velocity** → `uᵧ = u sinθ` *(changes due to gravity)*

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas — Master These!

### 🔸 At any time **t**:

| Quantity | Formula | Trick to Remember |
|----------|---------|------------------|
| Horizontal velocity | `vₓ = u cosθ` | Never changes! |
| Vertical velocity | `vᵧ = u sinθ - gt` | Standard v = u - at |
| Horizontal displacement | `x = u cosθ · t` | Simple = speed × time |
| Vertical displacement | `y = u sinθ · t - ½gt²` | Standard s = ut - ½gt² |

---

### 🔸 The Big Four — Most Tested in NEET:

#### ① Time of Flight (T)
$$T = \frac{2u\sinθ}{g}$$
> *Time for projectile to return to same horizontal level*

#### ② Maximum Height (H)
$$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2θ}{2g}$$
> *Highest point reached above launch level*

#### ③ Horizontal Range (R)
$$R = \frac{u^2\sin2θ}{g}$$
> *Horizontal distance covered when it lands*

#### ④ Equation of Trajectory (Shape of path)
$$y = x\tanθ - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2θ}$$
> *This is a **parabola** — confirms the curved path*

---

### 🔸 Special Angle Results (Frequently Tested!):

```
🎯 Maximum Range → θ = 45°     → R_max = u²/g

🎯 Same Range for two angles → θ and (90° - θ)
   Example: 30° and 60° give SAME range!

🎯 At Highest Point:
   • Vertical velocity = 0
   • Horizontal velocity = u cosθ (still present!)
   • Speed is MINIMUM (not zero, unless θ = 90°)
   • KE is MINIMUM, PE is MAXIMUM
```

---

## 3. 📋 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: **"Find the angle for maximum range"**
> Always **θ = 45°** → R = u²/g
> *(Direct 1-mark question)*

---

### Pattern 2: **"Two angles giving same range"**
> If R is same for θ₁ and θ₂, then **θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°**
> *Example: 20° & 70°, 30° & 60°, 25° & 65°*

---

### Pattern 3: **"Velocity/Speed at highest point"**
> At maximum height:
> - **vᵧ = 0** (vertical becomes zero)
> - **vₓ = u cosθ** (horizontal remains)
> - **Speed = u cosθ** (minimum speed during flight)

---

### Pattern 4: **"Ratio of H to R"**
$$\frac{H}{R} = \frac{\tan θ}{4}$$
> Very commonly asked — memorize this derived result!

---

### Pattern 5: **"Projectile from a height / horizontal projection"**
> Ball thrown *horizontally* (θ = 0°):
> - `uₓ = u`, `uᵧ = 0`
> - Time to fall height h: **t = √(2h/g)**
> - Range: **R = u × √(2h/g)**

---

### Pattern 6: **"Comparing KE/PE at different points"**
> At highest point:
> $$KE_{top} = \frac{1}{2}m(u\cosθ)^2 = KE_{initial} \times \cos^2θ$$

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tips & Analogies

### 🏏 The Cricket Analogy:
> Think of a **cricket ball hit at an angle** — it goes up (vertical component fighting gravity) while moving forward (horizontal component constant). The ball doesn't know about height — it just keeps moving sideways at the same speed!

---

### 🧲 The "Elevator" Trick:
> Imagine the projectile is in an **elevator moving horizontally at constant speed**. Inside, the ball just goes straight up and comes straight down. That's the vertical component. The horizontal movement is the elevator moving forward. Both happen *simultaneously* but *independently!*

---

### 📝 Formula Memory Mnemonics:

```
T = 2u sinθ/g    →  "Two Ugly Snakes Guard"  (2, u, sin, g)
H = u²sin²θ/2g  →  H has TWO sin's and a 2 below
R = u²sin2θ/g   →  R has sin of DOUBLE angle (2θ)
```

### ⚡ Quick Relationship:
$$R = 4H\cotθ \quad \text{and} \quad T^2 = \frac{8H}{g}$$

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem (NEET-Style)

### Question:
> A ball is projected with a velocity of **20 m/s** at an angle of **30°** with the horizontal. Find:
> (a) Time of flight
> (b) Maximum height
> (c) Horizontal range
> *(Take g = 10 m/s²)*

---

### ✅ Solution:

**Given:**
- u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s²
- sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866
- sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866

---

**Step 1: Find components**
```
uₓ = u cosθ = 20 × cos30° = 20 × (√3/2) = 10√3 m/s
uᵧ = u sinθ = 20 × sin30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s
```

---

**Step 2: Time of Flight (T)**
$$T = \frac{2u\sinθ}{g} = \frac{2 × 20 × \sin30°}{10} = \frac{2 × 20 × 0.5}{10}$$
$$\boxed{T = \frac{20}{10} = 2 \text{ seconds}}$$

---

**Step 3: Maximum Height (H)**
$$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2θ}{2g} = \frac{(20)^2 × (\sin30°)^2}{2 × 10} = \frac{400 × 0.25}{20}$$
$$\boxed{H = \frac{100}{20} = 5 \text{ metres}}$$

---

**Step 4: Horizontal Range (R)**
$$R = \frac{u^2\sin2θ}{g} = \frac{(20)^2 × \sin60°}{10} = \frac{400 × \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{10}$$
$$\boxed{R = \frac{200\sqrt{3}}{10} = 20\sqrt{3} ≈ 34.6 \text{ metres}}$$

---

**Verification Check** ✓
```
Also: R = uₓ × T = 10√3 × 2 = 20√3 ✓ (Both methods match!)
```

---

## 🔖 Quick Revision Card

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║           PROJECTILE MOTION — NEET SNAPSHOT          ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  T = 2u sinθ/g      → depends on vertical only      ║
║  H = u²sin²θ/2g     → depends on vertical only      ║
║  R = u²sin2θ/g      → depends on BOTH components    ║
║  Max R at θ = 45°   → R_max = u²/g                  ║
║  Same R: θ & (90-θ) → complementary angles          ║
║  At top: speed = u cosθ (minimum, not zero!)         ║
║  Trajectory = Parabola always

# Uniform Circular Motion (UCM)
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

**Uniform Circular Motion** is the motion of an object moving along a **circular path** with a **constant speed**.

> ⚠️ Key Distinction: Speed is constant, but **velocity is NOT constant** — because direction changes continuously.

Since velocity changes → there IS acceleration → there IS a net force acting on the body.

### What's Changing vs. What's Constant:

| Quantity | Status | Reason |
|----------|--------|--------|
| Speed | ✅ Constant | Magnitude unchanged |
| Velocity | ❌ Not constant | Direction changes |
| Acceleration | ❌ Not constant | Direction changes |
| Kinetic Energy | ✅ Constant | Speed is constant |
| Angular velocity (ω) | ✅ Constant | Uniform motion |

---

### The Direction of Acceleration & Force:

The acceleration in UCM always points **toward the center** of the circle.
This is called **Centripetal Acceleration**.

> 🎯 "Centripetal" = Center-seeking (from Latin: *centrum* = center, *petere* = to seek)

The force causing this = **Centripetal Force** (also directed toward center).

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas

### 🔹 Angular Velocity (ω):
$$\omega = \frac{\theta}{t} = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f$$

- T = Time period (time for one full revolution)
- f = Frequency (revolutions per second)

---

### 🔹 Linear Speed (v):
$$v = r\omega = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$$

---

### 🔹 Centripetal Acceleration (aᶜ):
$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

**Direction** → Always toward the center (centripetal)

---

### 🔹 Centripetal Force (Fᶜ):
$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$$

> ⚠️ **NEET TRAP**: Centripetal force is NOT a new type of force. It is provided BY existing forces:
> - Tension (stone in a string)
> - Gravity (moon around Earth)
> - Normal force (car on a curved road)
> - Friction (car turning on flat road)

---

### 🔹 Time Period & Frequency:
$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$$
$$f = \frac{1}{T}$$

---

### 🔹 Relationship Summary:
```
ω → v = rω → aᶜ = v²/r → Fᶜ = mv²/r
```

---

## 3. 📝 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Finding centripetal acceleration or force
> *"A particle moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with speed 2 m/s. Find centripetal acceleration."*
→ Direct formula application: aᶜ = v²/r

---

### Pattern 2: Direction of velocity/acceleration
> *"In UCM, which quantity remains constant?"*
→ Remember: **Speed, KE, angular velocity** remain constant; velocity, acceleration, momentum do NOT.

---

### Pattern 3: What provides centripetal force?
> *"A car moves on a curved road — what provides centripetal force?"*
→ **Friction** between tires and road

---

### Pattern 4: Doubling radius or speed
> *"If speed is doubled, radius kept same — what happens to centripetal force?"*
→ Fᶜ = mv²/r → F becomes **4 times** (v² dependence!)

---

### Pattern 5: Vertical circles (advanced)
> *"A stone is whirled in a vertical circle — minimum speed at top?"*
→ At top: mg = mv²/r → v_min = √(gr)

---

### ⚡ Concept Questions Often Asked in NEET:
- Work done by centripetal force = **ZERO** (force ⊥ displacement always)
- Centripetal force and centrifugal force are **NOT action-reaction pairs**
- In UCM, the **net tangential acceleration = 0** (speed doesn't change)

---

## 4. 🧠 Memory Tips & Analogies

### Analogy 1: The Hammer Throw Athlete
When an athlete swings a hammer in a circle:
- **String tension** = Centripetal force (toward athlete's hand = center)
- If string breaks → hammer flies **tangentially** (not outward, not inward!)
- This proves: velocity in UCM is always **tangential** to the circle

---

### Analogy 2: Earth & Moon
Moon orbits Earth in (approximately) UCM:
- **Gravity** = Centripetal force
- Moon doesn't fall to Earth OR fly away → perfect balance!

---

### 🔑 Memory Formula Chain:
```
"Oscar Visits All Films Twice"
ω → v → aᶜ → Fᶜ → T
```

### Golden Rules to Remember:
> 1. **Speed constant ≠ Velocity constant**
> 2. **Centripetal force does ZERO work**
> 3. **Velocity is tangential; Force is radial (centripetal)**
> 4. **No centripetal force = No circular motion (object moves in straight line)**

---

## 5. 💡 Example Problem (NEET Style)

**Question:**
A stone of mass 0.5 kg is tied to a string of length 1 m and whirled in a horizontal circle with a speed of 4 m/s. Calculate:
(a) Angular velocity
(b) Centripetal acceleration
(c) Centripetal force

---

**Solution:**

**Given:**
- m = 0.5 kg
- r = 1 m
- v = 4 m/s

---

**(a) Angular Velocity:**
$$\omega = \frac{v}{r} = \frac{4}{1} = 4 \text{ rad/s}$$

---

**(b) Centripetal Acceleration:**
$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{(4)^2}{1} = \frac{16}{1} = 16 \text{ m/s}^2$$

*(Direction: toward the center of the circle)*

---

**(c) Centripetal Force:**
$$F_c = ma_c = 0.5 \times 16 = 8 \text{ N}$$

*OR directly:*
$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{0.5 \times 16}{1} = 8 \text{ N}$$

*(This force is provided by the **tension** in the string)*

---

**Answer:** ω = 4 rad/s | aᶜ = 16 m/s² | Fᶜ = 8 N ✅

---

## 📌 Quick Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         UCM — NEET CHEAT SHEET              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ v = rω          (linear & angular speed)    │
│ aᶜ = v²/r = ω²r (centripetal acceleration) │
│ Fᶜ = mv²/r      (centripetal force)         │
│ T = 2πr/v       (time period)               │
│ Work by Fᶜ = 0  (force ⊥ velocity)         │
│ Velocity → tangential                       │
│ Force → centripetal (inward)               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

> 💬 **Pro NEET Tip:** Every year, NEET asks 1-2 questions on UCM — mostly conceptual (direction of quantities, what remains constant) + one numerical. Master both and you won't lose these marks! 🎯

[NEET 2022 | Physics]

A projectile is thrown with velocity v making angle θ with the horizontal. The range of the projectile is same when the angle of projection is:
Motion in a Plane.solution:
## Answer: **(C) 90° − θ**

---

## Step-by-Step Explanation

### The Range Formula
For projectile motion, the horizontal range is:
$$R = \frac{v^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$$

### Finding When Ranges Are Equal
For two different angles to give the same range:
$$\sin(2\theta_1) = \sin(2\theta_2)$$

Using the property of sine function: **sin(A) = sin(B) when A + B = 180°**

$$2\theta + 2\theta_2 = 180°$$
$$\theta + \theta_2 = 90°$$
$$\theta_2 = 90° - \theta$$

---

## Verification

Let's check with a numerical example:
- **At θ = 30°:** sin(2 × 30°) = sin(60°) = √3/2
- **At θ = 60°:** sin(2 × 60°) = sin(120°) = √3/2 ✓

(Notice: 30° + 60° = 90°)

---

## Why Other Options Are Wrong

| Option | Why Wrong |
|--------|-----------|
| (A) 45° + θ | sin(2(45° + θ)) ≠ sin(2θ) in general |
| (B) 180° − θ | sin(2(180° − θ)) = sin(360° − 2θ) = −sin(2θ) ≠ sin(2θ) |
| (D) 90° + θ | sin(2(90° + θ)) = sin(180° + 2θ) = −sin(2θ) ≠ sin(2θ) |

---

## Key Concept to Remember 🎯

**Complementary Angle Rule for Projectile Range:**
Two angles θ and (90° − θ) give the **same range** when projected with the same initial velocity.

This is why 30° and 60°, or 15° and 75°, all give identical ranges!

# Multiplication of Vectors by Real Numbers
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🎯 Core Concept and Definition

When a vector **A** is multiplied by a real number (scalar) **λ**, the result is a **new vector** whose:

| Property | Result |
|----------|--------|
| **Magnitude** | \|λ\| × \|**A**\| |
| **Direction** | Same as **A** if λ > 0 |
| **Direction** | Opposite to **A** if λ < 0 |
| **Nature** | Same physical quantity as **A** |

> **In simple words:** Multiplying a vector by a number **stretches, shrinks, or flips** it — but it remains the *same type* of vector.

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas and Important Facts

### Basic Expression:
$$\vec{B} = \lambda\vec{A}$$

Where:
$$|\vec{B}| = |\lambda| \times |\vec{A}|$$

---

### 🔑 Three Critical Cases:

**Case 1: λ > 1 (e.g., λ = 3)**
```
A  →→
B  →→→→→→  (longer, same direction)
```
$$|\vec{B}| > |\vec{A}|, \text{ same direction}$$

---

**Case 2: 0 < λ < 1 (e.g., λ = 0.5)**
```
A  →→→→
B  →→    (shorter, same direction)
```
$$|\vec{B}| < |\vec{A}|, \text{ same direction}$$

---

**Case 3: λ < 0 (e.g., λ = -1)**
```
A  →→→→
B  ←←←←  (reversed direction)
```
$$|\vec{B}| = |\vec{A}|, \text{ opposite direction}$$

> ⚠️ **Special case:** When **λ = -1**, we get the **negative of vector A**
> $$(-1)\vec{A} = -\vec{A}$$
> This is the **additive inverse** of **A**

---

### 📌 Important Facts to Remember:

| Fact | Detail |
|------|--------|
| Unit vector | $\hat{A} = \dfrac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$, here λ = $\dfrac{1}{|\vec{A}|}$ |
| λ = 0 | Gives a **null/zero vector** |
| Physical dimension | Same as original vector |
| Distributive law | $\lambda(\vec{A} + \vec{B}) = \lambda\vec{A} + \lambda\vec{B}$ |
| Associative law | $(\lambda_1\lambda_2)\vec{A} = \lambda_1(\lambda_2\vec{A})$ |

---

## 3. 📝 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Unit Vector Formation
> *"Find a unit vector in the direction of 3î + 4ĵ"*

This directly uses **λ = 1/|A|** concept.

---

### Pattern 2: Negative Vector
> *"If **F** = 5N eastward, what is **-2F**?"*

Answer: 10N **westward** (magnitude doubles, direction flips)

---

### Pattern 3: Conceptual True/False
> *"When a vector is multiplied by a negative scalar, only its direction changes"*

**TRUE** — magnitude uses |λ|, so magnitude = |(-2)| × |A| = 2|A| *(magnitude also changes here!)*

> ⚠️ **NEET Trap:** If λ = -1, only direction changes. If λ = any other negative number, BOTH magnitude and direction change!

---

### Pattern 4: Component-wise multiplication
> *"If **A** = 2î + 3ĵ, find 4**A**"*

$$4\vec{A} = 4(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}) = 8\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$$

---

## 4. 🧠 Memory Tip / Analogy

### 🚶 The Walking Analogy:
Think of a vector as **your step** (1 step forward = 1 unit east)

| Multiplication | Real Life |
|----------------|-----------|
| 3 × (1 step East) | Take 3 steps East |
| 0.5 × (1 step East) | Take half a step East |
| -1 × (1 step East) | Take 1 step **West** |
| -3 × (1 step East) | Take 3 steps **West** |

---

### 🎯 Golden Rule to Remember:
$$\boxed{\text{Sign of λ} \rightarrow \text{Controls Direction} \quad | \quad |\lambda| \rightarrow \text{Controls Magnitude}}$$

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem with Solution

### Problem:
> A force vector is given as **F** = (3î + 4ĵ) N.
> **(a)** Find the magnitude of **F**
> **(b)** Find the unit vector along **F**
> **(c)** Find a vector of magnitude 10N in the direction opposite to **F**

---

### Solution:

**Step 1: Find magnitude**
$$|\vec{F}| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \text{ N}$$

---

**Step 2: Find unit vector (using scalar multiplication with λ = 1/5)**
$$\hat{F} = \frac{\vec{F}}{|\vec{F}|} = \frac{1}{5}(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})$$
$$\boxed{\hat{F} = 0.6\hat{i} + 0.8\hat{j}}$$

*Verify: $\sqrt{0.6^2 + 0.8^2} = \sqrt{0.36 + 0.64} = \sqrt{1} = 1$ ✅*

---

**Step 3: Vector of magnitude 10N in opposite direction**

We need: magnitude = 10N, direction = opposite to **F**

$$\vec{F}_{new} = -2\vec{F} = -2(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})$$
$$\boxed{\vec{F}_{new} = -6\hat{i} - 8\hat{j} \text{ N}}$$

*Here λ = **-2** → magnitude becomes 2×5 = 10N ✅, direction reversed ✅*

---

## 🔖 Quick Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  λA = vector with magnitude |λ||A|           │
│  λ > 0 → same direction                     │
│  λ < 0 → opposite direction                 │
│  λ = 0 → null vector                        │
│  λ = -1 → additive inverse (-A)             │
│  Unit vector = A/|A|  [λ = 1/|A|]           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

> 💡 **NEET Tip:** Unit vector problems appear almost **every year** in NEET. Master the formula $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$ — it's a direct application of scalar multiplication!

# Vector Addition — Analytical Method
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

When two or more vectors act on a body **at an angle**, we cannot simply add their magnitudes. The **analytical method** (also called the **component method**) gives us an **exact mathematical result** — unlike the graphical method which is approximate.

### The Big Idea:
> **Break every vector into its horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components, add components separately, then reconstruct the resultant.**

Think of it like this:
- A vector is like a **journey with two parts** — how far East and how far North.
- You add all "Easts" together and all "Norths" together.
- Then find your total displacement using Pythagoras.

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas

### Step 1: Resolve each vector into components

For a vector **A** making angle **θ** with the x-axis:

$$\boxed{A_x = A\cos\theta \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta}$$

---

### Step 2: Add components along each axis

$$R_x = A_x + B_x = A\cos\theta_1 + B\cos\theta_2$$

$$R_y = A_y + B_y = A\sin\theta_1 + B\sin\theta_2$$

---

### Step 3: Find magnitude of resultant

$$\boxed{R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}}$$

---

### Step 4: Find direction of resultant

$$\boxed{\tan\alpha = \frac{R_y}{R_x}}$$

where **α** is the angle the resultant makes with the x-axis.

---

### ⭐ Special Case — Two Vectors at Angle θ Between Them:

$$\boxed{R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}}$$

$$\boxed{\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}}$$

> This is the **Parallelogram Law in formula form** — extremely important for NEET!

---

## 3. 🎯 Common NEET Question Patterns

| Pattern | What's Asked | Key Trick |
|---|---|---|
| Two forces at given angle | Find resultant magnitude | Use $\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$ |
| Resultant is perpendicular to one vector | Find angle between vectors | Use $\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}$; set α = 90° |
| Maximum & Minimum resultant | Find R_max and R_min | R_max = A+B (θ=0°), R_min = |A-B| (θ=180°) |
| Resultant equals either vector | Find angle | Use the formula and equate R = A or R = B |
| Three vectors in equilibrium | Find unknown vector | Sum of all components = 0 |

### 🔑 Critical Values to Memorize:

| Angle (θ) | cos θ | Resultant R |
|---|---|---|
| 0° | +1 | A + B (Maximum) |
| 60° | +1/2 | $\sqrt{A^2+B^2+AB}$ |
| 90° | 0 | $\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$ |
| 120° | -1/2 | $\sqrt{A^2+B^2-AB}$ |
| 180° | -1 | \|A - B\| (Minimum) |

---

## 4. 🧠 Memory Tip & Analogy

### The "GPS Navigation" Analogy:
Imagine Google Maps telling you:
- "Go **4 km East** and **3 km North**"

It doesn't tell you to go diagonally — it breaks the path into components!
The straight-line distance = $\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2}$ = **5 km** ← That's your resultant!

### Formula Memory Trick — **"RASTA"**:
- **R**esolve into components
- **A**dd x-components → R_x
- **S**um y-components → R_y
- **T**ake square root → Magnitude
- **A**rctangent → Direction

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem (NEET Style)

**Question:**
Two forces of **6 N** and **8 N** act on a body at right angles to each other. Find:
(a) The magnitude of the resultant force
(b) The angle it makes with the 6 N force

---

**Solution:**

**Given:**
- A = 6 N, B = 8 N
- θ = 90° (angle between them)

---

**Step 1:** Find magnitude using the resultant formula:

$$R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$$

$$R = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2 + 2(6)(8)\cos 90°}$$

$$R = \sqrt{36 + 64 + 0} \quad [\because \cos 90° = 0]$$

$$\boxed{R = \sqrt{100} = 10 \text{ N}}$$

---

**Step 2:** Find direction (angle with 6 N force):

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta} = \frac{8\sin 90°}{6 + 8\cos 90°}$$

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{8 \times 1}{6 + 0} = \frac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3}$$

$$\boxed{\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx 53°}$$

**Answer:** The resultant is **10 N** at **53° from the 6 N force**

---

> 💡 **Pro Tip:** This 6-8-10 is a Pythagorean triplet! In NEET, when two vectors are perpendicular, always check for Pythagorean triplets (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17) — saves calculation time!

---

## 📌 Quick Revision Box

```
✅ R = √(A² + B² + 2ABcosθ)      ← Magnitude
✅ tanα = Bsinθ / (A + Bcosθ)    ← Direction  
✅ R_max = A + B  (at θ = 0°)
✅ R_min = |A - B| (at θ = 180°)
✅ For θ = 90°: R = √(A² + B²)
✅ Components: Aₓ = Acosθ, Aᵧ = Asinθ
```

---

*Master this topic and you can handle projectile motion, relative velocity, and equilibrium of forces — all in Chapter 4 and beyond!* 🚀

Motion in a Plane.question: Two bodies of mass $$1 \mathrm{~kg}$$ and $$3 \mathrm{~kg}$$ have position vectors $$\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$$ and $$-3 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$$ respectively. The magnitude of position vector of centre of mass of this system will be similar to the magnitude of vector :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$${\overline r _{com}} = {{{m_1}{{\overline r }_1} + {m_2}{{\overline r }_2}} \over {{m_1} + {m_2}}}$$

$$ = {{(1 - 9)\widehat i + (2 - 6)\widehat j + (1 + 3)\widehat k} \over 4}$$

$$ = {{ - 8\widehat i - 4\widehat j + 4\widehat k} \over 4}$$

$${\overline r _{com}} = - 2\widehat i - \widehat j + \widehat k$$

$$\left| {\overline r } \right| = \sqrt {4 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt 6 $$

$$\left| {\widehat i + 2\widehat j + \widehat k} \right| = \sqrt 6 $$

The magnetic flux through the area of the circular coil area is given by $$\phi $$<sub>0</sub>. Which of the following option is correct?

in opposite direction hence $$\phi $$<sub>i</sub> = - $$\phi $$<sub>0</sub>.

Motion in a Plane.question: An aeroplane, with its wings spread 10 m, is flying at a speed of 180 km/h in a horizontal direction. The total intensity of earth's field at that part is 2.5 $$\times$$ 10<sup>$$-$$4</sup> Wb/m<sup>2</sup> and the angle of dip is 60$$^\circ$$. The emf induced between the tips of the plane wings will be __________.
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$$\varepsilon $$ind = (Bv) LV and Bv = BTotal sin60o

$$ \therefore $$ $$\varepsilon $$ind = (2.5 $$\times$$ 10$$-$$4)(sin 60o) $$\times$$ 10 $$\times$$ 180 $$\times$$ $${5 \over {18}}$$

= 108.25 mV
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question: Two guns A and B can fire bullets at speeds 1 km/s and 2 km/s respectively. From a point on a horizontal ground, they are fired in all possible directions. The ratio of maximum areas covered by the bullets fired by the two guns, on the ground is -
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$$R = {{{u^2}\sin 2\theta } \over g}$$

$$A = \pi \,{R^2}$$

$$A \propto {R^2}$$

$$A \propto {u^4}$$

$${{{A_1}} \over {{A_2}}} = {{u_1^4} \over {u_2^4}} = {\left[ {{1 \over 2}} \right]^4} = {1 \over {16}}$$
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question:
A shell is fired from a fixed artillery gun with an initial speed u such that it hits the target on the ground at a
distance R from it. If t<sub>1</sub> and t<sub>2</sub> are the values of the time taken by it to hit the target in two possible ways, the
product t<sub>1</sub>t<sub>2</sub> is -
Motion in a Plane.solution:
Range will be same for time t1 and t2, so angles of projection will be ‘$$\theta $$’ & ‘90° – $$\theta $$’

$${t_1} = {{2u\sin \theta } \over g}{t_2} = {{2u\sin \left( {{{90}^o} - \theta } \right)} \over g}$$

and $$R = {{{u^2}\sin 2\theta } \over g}$$

$${t_1}{t_2} = {{4{u^2}\sin \theta \cos \theta } \over {{g^2}}} = {2 \over g}\left[ {{{2{u^2}\sin \theta \cos \theta } \over g}} \right]$$

= $${{2R} \over g}$$
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question:
Two particles are projected from the same point with the same speed u such that they have the same range R,
but different maximum heights, h<sub>1</sub> and h<sub>2</sub>. Which of the following is correct ?
Motion in a Plane.solution:
The range of two particles are same, that means angle of projections must be complementary to each other.

So one angle = $$\theta $$ and other one is = 90o - $$\theta $$

R = $${{{u^2}\sin 2\theta } \over g}$$ = $${{2{u^2}\sin \theta \cos \theta } \over g}$$

$$ \therefore $$ R2 = $${{4{u^4}{{\sin }^2}\theta {{\cos }^2}\theta } \over {{g^2}}}$$

h1 = $${{{u^2}{{\sin }^2}\theta } \over {2g}}$$

h2 = $${{{u^2}{{\sin }^2}\left( {{{90}^o} - \theta } \right)} \over {2g}}$$ = $${{{u^2}{{\cos }^2}\theta } \over {2g}}$$

h1h2 = $${{{u^4}{{\sin }^2}\theta {{\cos }^2}\theta } \over {4{g^2}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ h1h2 = $${{{R^2}} \over {16}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ R2 = 16 h1h2
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question: The trajectory of a projectile in a vertical plane is y = $$\alpha$$x $$-$$ $$\beta$$x<sup>2</sup>, where $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ are constants and x & y are respectively the horizontal and vertical distances of the projectile from the point of projection. The angle of projection $$\theta$$ and the maximum height attained H are respectively given by :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
y = $$\alpha$$x $$-$$ $$\beta$$x2

comparing with trajectory equation

$$y = x\tan \theta - {1 \over 2}{{g{x^2}} \over {{u^2}{{\cos }^2}\theta }}$$

$$\tan \theta = \alpha \Rightarrow \theta = {\tan ^{ - 1}}\alpha $$

$$\beta = {1 \over 2}{g \over {{u^2}{{\cos }^2}\theta }}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${u^2} = {g \over {2\beta {{\cos }^2}\theta }}$$

Maximum height H :

$$H = {{{u^2}{{\sin }^2}\theta } \over {2g}} = {g \over {2\beta {{\cos }^2}\theta }}{{{{\sin }^2}\theta } \over {2g}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$H = {{{{\tan }^2}\theta } \over {4\beta }} = {{{\alpha ^2}} \over {4\beta }}$$
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question: A bomb is dropped by fighter plane flying horizontally. To an observer sitting in the plane, the trajectory of the bomb is a :

options.B: parabola in the direction of motion of plane
options.C: straight line vertically down the plane
options.D: parabola in a direction opposite to the motion of plane

Motion in a Plane.solution:
The correct answer is Option C, a straight line vertically down the plane.

Here's why:

  • Frame of Reference: The key to understanding projectile motion is considering the frame of reference. The observer in the plane is in a moving frame of reference. From their perspective, they are at rest, and the bomb has the same horizontal velocity as the plane.

  • Gravity's Influence: The only force acting on the bomb after it's released is gravity. Gravity acts vertically downwards.

  • Resultant Motion: Because the bomb has the same horizontal velocity as the plane and is only affected by gravity vertically, it appears to the observer in the plane to fall straight down.

Let's eliminate the other options:

  • Option A (Hyperbola): A hyperbolic trajectory occurs when an object is influenced by two forces acting in different directions, resulting in a path that gets progressively straighter. This doesn't apply to the bomb scenario.

  • Option B and D (Parabola): A parabolic trajectory is observed from a stationary frame of reference on the ground. In this case, the horizontal motion of the bomb combined with the vertical acceleration due to gravity creates a parabolic path.
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question: The ranges and heights for two projectiles projected with the same initial velocity at angles 42$$^\circ$$ and 48$$^\circ$$ with the horizontal are R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>1</sub>, H<sub>2</sub> respectively. Choose the correct option :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
Here, two projectiles are projected at angles 42$$^\circ$$ and 48$$^\circ$$ with same initial velocity.

As we know the expression of range of projectile,

Range $$ = {{{u^2}\sin 2\theta } \over g}$$

AT $$\theta$$1 = 42$$^\circ$$,

Range, $${R_1} = {{{u^2}\sin 2(42)^\circ } \over g} = {{0.99{u^2}} \over g}$$

At $$\theta$$2 = 48$$^\circ$$

Range, $${R_2} = {{{u^2}\sin 2(48)^\circ } \over g} = {{0.99{u^2}} \over g}$$

The range of the projectile is same for the two projectiles.

Therefore, R1 = R2

Now, as we know the expression of height of the projectile,

$${H_{\max }} = {{{u^2}\sin \theta } \over {2g}}$$

At 42$$^\circ$$, $${H_{\max }} = {H_1} = {{{u^2}\sin 42^\circ } \over {2g}} = {{0.669{u^2}} \over {2g}}$$

At 48$$^\circ$$, $${H_{\max }} = {H_2} = {{{u^2}\sin 48^\circ } \over {2g}} = {{0.743{u^2}} \over {2g}}$$

Higher the value of $$\theta$$ higher the value of maximum height. Therefore, H1 < H2.
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question: A person can throw a ball upto a maximum range of 100 m. How high above the ground he can throw the same ball?
Motion in a Plane.solution:
To determine how high a person can throw a ball given the maximum range, we need to use the principles of projectile motion in physics. The maximum range of a projectile is given by the formula:

$$ R = \frac{{v_0^2 \sin(2\theta)}}{g} $$

where:

  • $$ R $$ is the range
  • $$ v_0 $$ is the initial velocity
  • $$ \theta $$ is the angle of projection
  • $$ g $$ is the acceleration due to gravity (approximately $$ 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2 $$)

The maximum range is achieved when $$ \theta = 45^\circ $$, thus $$ \sin(2\theta) = \sin(90^\circ) = 1 $$.

Given that the maximum range $$ R = 100 \, \text{m} $$, we can rewrite the range formula as:

$$ 100 = \frac{{v_0^2 \cdot 1}}{9.8} $$

Solving for $$ v_0^2 $$:

$$ v_0^2 = 100 \times 9.8 = 980 $$

Next, the maximum height $$ H $$ reached by the ball can be calculated using the vertical component of the velocity. The formula for the maximum height is:

$$ H = \frac{{v_0^2 \sin^2(\theta)}}{2g} $$

Here, for a vertical throw, $$ \theta = 90^\circ $$, and thus $$ \sin(90^\circ) = 1 $$.

Substituting the values, we get:

$$ H = \frac{{v_0^2 \cdot 1}}{2 \cdot 9.8} $$

Using $$ v_0^2 = 980 $$, we have:

$$ H = \frac{980}{2 \times 9.8} = \frac{980}{19.6} = 50 \, \text{m} $$

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option B: 50 m
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question: A projectile is launched at an angle '$$\alpha$$' with the horizontal with a velocity 20 ms$$-$$1. After 10 s, its inclination with horizontal is '$$\beta$$'. The value of tan$$\beta$$ will be : (g = 10 ms$$-$$2).
Motion in a Plane.solution:
At $t=0$, the motion of projectile is given as



$\tan \alpha=\frac{u_{y}}{u_{x}}$

where, $u_{y}$ is the vertical component of initial velocity and $u_{x}$ is the horizontal component of initial velocity.

At $t=10 \mathrm{~s}$, the motion of projectile is given as



$\tan \beta=\frac{v_{y}}{v_{x}}$ .........(ii)

where, $v_{y}$ is the vertical component of final velocity after $t=10 \mathrm{~s}$ and $v_{x}$ is the horizontal component of final velocity.

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{\tan \beta}{\tan \alpha}=\frac{v_y}{u_y} \quad\left(\right.$ as $v_x=u_x$ ) ....(iii)

Using the following equation in vertical direction, we get

$$ \begin{aligned} &v_{y}=u_{y}-g t \\\\ &v_{y}=u_{y}-100 \end{aligned} $$

Using Eq, (iii)}

$$ \frac{\tan \beta}{\tan \alpha}=\frac{u_{y}-100}{u_{y}} $$

$$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{\tan \beta}{\tan \alpha}=1-\frac{100}{u_{y}}=1-\frac{100}{20 \sin \alpha} \quad\left(\because u_{y}=20 \sin \alpha\right) \end{aligned} $$

$$ =1-\frac{5}{\sin \alpha} $$

$\Rightarrow \tan \beta=\tan \alpha\left(1-\frac{5}{\sin \alpha}\right)=\tan \alpha-5 \sec \alpha$
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question:
A projectile is projected with velocity of 25 m/s at an angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. After t seconds its inclination with horizontal becomes zero. If R represents horizontal range of the projectile, the value of $$\theta$$ will be :

[use g = 10 m/s2]
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$$t = {{25\sin \theta } \over g}$$

and, $$R = {{{{(25)}^2}(2\sin \theta \cos \theta )} \over g}$$

$$ \Rightarrow R = {{25 \times 25 \times 2} \over g} \times {{gt} \over {25}} \times \cos \theta $$

$$ \Rightarrow R = 50t\cos \theta $$

$$\therefore$$ $$tan\theta = {{gt} \over {25}} \times {{50t} \over R}$$

$$ = {{20{t^2}} \over R}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \theta = {\cot ^{ - 1}}\left( {{R \over {20{t^2}}}} \right)$$
Motion in a Plane.subject: Physics

Motion in a Plane.question: Two projectiles P1 and P2 thrown with speed in the ratio $$\sqrt3$$ : $$\sqrt2$$, attain the same height during their motion. If P2 is thrown at an angle of 60$$^\circ$$ with the horizontal, the angle of projection of P1 with horizontal will be :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
We know,

Maximum height of a projectile $$(H) = {{{u^2}{{\sin }^2}\theta } \over {2g}}$$

Given, Ratio of initial velocity of two projectile

$${{{u_1}} \over {{u_2}}} = {{\sqrt 3 } \over {\sqrt 2 }}$$

Both projectile reach the same maximum height.

$$\therefore$$ $${H_1} = {H_2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{u_1^2{{\sin }^2}{\theta _1}} \over {2g}} = {{u_2^2{{\sin }^2}{\theta _2}} \over {2g}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow u_1^2{\sin ^2}{\theta _1} = u_2^2{\sin ^2}{\theta _2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\left( {{{{u_1}} \over {{u_2}}}} \right)^2} = {\left( {{{\sin {\theta _2}} \over {\sin {\theta _1}}}} \right)^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\left( {{{\sqrt 3 } \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right)^2} = {\left( {{{\sin 60^\circ } \over {\sin {\theta _1}}}} \right)^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {3 \over 2} = {3 \over {4{{\sin }^2}{\theta _1}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \sin _{{\theta _1}}^2 = {1 \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \sin {\theta _1} = {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }} = \sin 45^\circ $$

$$ \Rightarrow {\theta _1} = 45^\circ $$

Motion in a Plane.question:
A ball is projected from the ground with a speed 15 ms$$-$$1 at an angle $$\theta$$ with horizontal so that its range and maximum height are equal,
then 'tan $$\theta$$' will be equal to :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
To solve this problem, we will use the equations for the range and maximum height of a projectile. The range $$R$$ and maximum height $$H$$ of a projectile launched with speed $$u$$ at an angle $$\theta$$ can be expressed as follows:

Range:

$$R = \frac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$$

Maximum height:

$$H = \frac{u^2 \sin^2(\theta)}{2g}$$

We are given that the range and maximum height are equal. So, we set these equations equal to each other:

$$\frac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g} = \frac{u^2 \sin^2(\theta)}{2g}$$

We can cancel out the common terms $$u^2$$ and $$g$$ on both sides:

$$\sin(2\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \sin^2(\theta)$$

Using the double angle identity for sine, $$\sin(2\theta) = 2 \sin(\theta) \cos(\theta)$$, we substitute it into the equation:

$$2 \sin(\theta) \cos(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \sin^2(\theta)$$

We can simplify this by dividing both sides by $$\sin(\theta)$$ (assuming $$\theta \neq 0$$):

$$2 \cos(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \sin(\theta)$$

Rearranging to get all terms on one side gives us:

$$4 \cos(\theta) = \sin(\theta)$$

Dividing both sides by $$\cos(\theta)$$, we get:

$$4 = \tan(\theta)$$

So, we find that:

$$\tan(\theta) = 4$$

Thus, the correct answer is:

Option D: 4

Motion in a Plane.question: Two projectiles are thrown with same initial velocity making an angle of $$45^{\circ}$$ and $$30^{\circ}$$ with the horizontal respectively. The ratio of their respective ranges will be :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
Here's how to determine the ratio of the ranges for the two projectiles:

Understanding the Concepts

  • Projectile Motion: Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown or projected into the air, subject to only the acceleration of gravity. The object is called a projectile, and its path is called its trajectory.

  • Range: The range of a projectile is the horizontal distance it covers from its launch point to the point where it returns to the same vertical height.

Key Formula

The formula for the range (R) of a projectile is:

$$R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$$

where:

  • R = Range

  • u = Initial velocity (same for both projectiles)

  • θ = Angle of projection

  • g = Acceleration due to gravity (constant)

Calculations

  1. Projectile 1 (45° angle):

Let the range of the projectile launched at 45° be R1.

$$R_1 = \frac{u^2 \sin (2 \times 45^{\circ})}{g} = \frac{u^2 \sin 90^{\circ}}{g} = \frac{u^2}{g} $$

  1. Projectile 2 (30° angle):

Let the range of the projectile launched at 30° be R2.

$$R_2 = \frac{u^2 \sin (2 \times 30^{\circ})}{g} = \frac{u^2 \sin 60^{\circ}}{g} = \frac{u^2 \sqrt{3}}{2g}$$

  1. Ratio of Ranges (R1 : R2):

Divide the range of projectile 1 by the range of projectile 2:

$$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{\frac{u^2}{g}}{\frac{u^2 \sqrt{3}}{2g}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$$

To simplify the ratio, multiply both numerator and denominator by √3:

$$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{2\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}}{3 \times \sqrt{3}} = \frac{6}{3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$$

Therefore, the ratio of the ranges of the two projectiles is 2 : √3, which corresponds to Option C.

Motion in a Plane.question: Two objects are projected with same velocity 'u' however at different angles $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ with the horizontal. If $$\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$$, the ratio of horizontal range of the first object to the 2nd object will be :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$$ \text {Range}=\frac{u^2 \sin 2 \theta}{g} $$

Range for projection angle " $\alpha$ "

$$ \mathrm{R}_1=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}} $$

Range for projection angle " $\beta$ "

$$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \beta}{\mathrm{g}} \\\\ & \alpha+\beta=90^{\circ}(\text { Given }) \\\\ & \Rightarrow \beta=90^{\circ}-\alpha \\\\ & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2\left(90^{\circ}-\alpha\right)}{\mathrm{g}} \\\\ & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin \left(180^{\circ}-2 \alpha\right)}{\mathrm{g}} \\\\ & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}} \\\\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\frac{\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}}\right)}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}}\right)}=\frac{1}{1} \end{aligned} $$

Motion in a Plane.question: The maximum vertical height to which a man can throw a ball is 136 m. The maximum horizontal distance upto which he can throw the same ball is :

Motion in a Plane.question: A projectile is projected at $$30^{\circ}$$ from horizontal with initial velocity $$40 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$$. The velocity of the projectile at $$\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$$ from the start will be : (Given $$g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$$ )
Motion in a Plane.solution:
To find the velocity of the projectile at t = 2 s, we need to find the horizontal and vertical components of the velocity at that time.

The initial horizontal component of the velocity is constant and is given by:

$$ v_{0x} = v_0 \cos\theta = 40\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} \cos(30^{\circ}) = 40\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 20\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} $$

The initial vertical component of the velocity is:

$$ v_{0y} = v_0 \sin\theta = 40\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} \sin(30^{\circ}) = 40\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 20\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} $$

To find the vertical component of the velocity at t = 2 s, we use the equation:

$$ v_y = v_{0y} - gt = 20\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} - (10\,\mathrm{ms}^{-2})(2\,\mathrm{s}) = 20\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} - 20\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} = 0\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} $$

At t = 2 s, the horizontal component of the velocity is still $$20\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$$, and the vertical component is 0. The overall velocity at t = 2 s is:

$$ \vec{v} = 20\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} \hat{i} + 0\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} \hat{j} = 20\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} $$

So the correct answer is: $$ 20\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{ms}^{-1} $$

Motion in a Plane.question: Two projectiles are projected at $$30^{\circ}$$ and $$60^{\circ}$$ with the horizontal with the same speed. The ratio of the maximum height attained by the two projectiles respectively is:
Motion in a Plane.solution:
Let the initial speed of both projectiles be v. The maximum height attained by a projectile can be calculated using the formula:

$$H = \frac{v^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$$

where H is the maximum height, v is the initial speed, θ is the angle of projection, and g is the acceleration due to gravity.

For the projectile projected at 30°, the maximum height is:

$$H_1 = \frac{v^2 \sin^2 30^{\circ}}{2g} = \frac{v^2 \times \frac{1}{4}}{2g} = \frac{v^2}{8g}$$

For the projectile projected at 60°, the maximum height is:

$$H_2 = \frac{v^2 \sin^2 60^{\circ}}{2g} = \frac{v^2 \times \frac{3}{4}}{2g} = \frac{3v^2}{8g}$$

Now, let's find the ratio of the maximum heights:

$$\frac{H_1}{H_2} = \frac{\frac{v^2}{8g}}{\frac{3v^2}{8g}} = \frac{v^2}{3v^2}$$

The v² terms cancel out, and we get:

$$\frac{H_1}{H_2} = \frac{1}{3}$$

Therefore, the ratio of the maximum heights attained by the two projectiles is 1 : 3

Motion in a Plane.question: The range of the projectile projected at an angle of 15$$^\circ$$ with horizontal is 50 m. If the projectile is projected with same velocity at an angle of 45$$^\circ$$ with horizontal, then its range will be
Motion in a Plane.solution:
The range $R$ of a projectile launched with an initial speed $v$ and at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal is given by:

$R = \frac{v^2}{g} \sin(2\theta)$

where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

From this equation, we can see that the range is dependent on the sine of twice the launch angle.

Given that the range at $15^\circ$ is $50$ m, if we launch the projectile at $45^\circ$ with the same velocity, we can compare the ranges by comparing $\sin(2 \times 15^\circ)$ and $\sin(2 \times 45^\circ)$:

$\sin(30^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}$

$\sin(90^\circ) = 1$

Therefore, the range at $45^\circ$ will be twice the range at $15^\circ$, because $\sin(90^\circ)$ is twice as large as $\sin(30^\circ)$.

So, the range when the projectile is launched at $45^\circ$ will be $2 \times 50$ m = $100$ m.

So, $100$ m is the correct answer.

Motion in a Plane.question: Two projectiles A and B are thrown with initial velocities of $$40 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$$ and $$60 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$$ at angles $$30^{\circ}$$ and $$60^{\circ}$$ with the horizontal respectively. The ratio of their ranges respectively is $$\left(g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\right)$$
Motion in a Plane.solution:
The range of a projectile launched with an initial velocity $v$ at an angle $\theta$ with respect to the horizontal is given by:

$R = \frac{v^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$,

where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's calculate the ranges of projectiles A and B:

For projectile A, $v = 40 \, \text{m/s}$ and $\theta = 30^\circ$, so:

$R_A = \frac{(40)^2 \sin(2 \times 30)}{10} = 4 \times 40 = 160 \, \text{m}$.

For projectile B, $v = 60 \, \text{m/s}$ and $\theta = 60^\circ$, so:

$R_B = \frac{(60)^2 \sin(2 \times 60)}{10} = 6 \times 60 = 360 \, \text{m}$.

Therefore, the ratio of their ranges is $R_A : R_B = 160 : 360 = 4 : 9$.

Motion in a Plane.question:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A : When a body is projected at an angle $$45^{\circ}$$, it's range is maximum.

Reason R : For maximum range, the value of $$\sin 2 \theta$$ should be equal to one.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.A: Both $$\mathbf{A}$$ and $$\mathbf{R}$$ are correct and $$\mathbf{R}$$ is the correct explanation of $$\mathbf{A}$$
options.D: Both $$\mathbf{A}$$ and $$\mathbf{R}$$ are correct but $$\mathbf{R}$$ is NOT the correct explanation of $$\mathbf{A}$$

Motion in a Plane.solution:
Assertion A: When a body is projected at an angle of $45^{\circ}$, its range is maximum. This is true, and it's a well-established fact in physics. The maximum range of a projectile, assuming no air resistance and flat terrain, is achieved at an angle of $45^{\circ}$.

Reason R: For maximum range, the value of $\sin 2\theta$ should be equal to one. This is also true. The range of a projectile, again assuming no air resistance and flat terrain, can be calculated using the formula $R = (v^{2}/g) \cdot \sin(2\theta)$, where $v$ is the initial velocity of the projectile, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, and $\theta$ is the launch angle. For the range to be maximized, $\sin(2\theta)$ must be maximized, and the maximum value of $\sin(2\theta)$ is 1. This occurs when $2\theta = 90$ degrees, or $\theta = 45$ degrees, which corresponds to the assertion.

Motion in a Plane.question:
The co-ordinates of a particle moving in $$x$$-$$y$$ plane are given by : $$x=2+4 \mathrm{t}, y=3 \mathrm{t}+8 \mathrm{t}^2$$.

The motion of the particle is :

options.A: uniform motion along a straight line.
options.C: uniformly accelerated having motion along a straight line.
options.D: uniformly accelerated having motion along a parabolic path.

Motion in a Plane.solution:
To determine the nature of the motion of the particle given by its coordinates in the $$x$$-$$y$$ plane, we analyze the given equations for $$x$$ and $$y$$ in terms of time $$t$$:

  • $$x = 2 + 4t$$
  • $$y = 3t + 8t^2$$

Firstly, the equation for $$x$$ is of the form $$x = x_0 + vt$$, where $$x_0 = 2$$ is the initial position and $$v = 4$$ is the constant velocity along the $$x$$-axis. This suggests a uniform motion along the $$x$$-axis because the velocity remains constant with time.

Secondly, the equation for $$y$$ is a second-degree polynomial in $$t$$, which indicates a parabolic path. The presence of the $$t^2$$ term ($$8t^2$$) signifies acceleration since the position along the $$y$$-axis is changing at a rate that itself changes over time.

The equation for $$y$$ can show two types of motion depending on the terms:

  1. If it was of the form $$y = y_0 + vt$$, it would indicate uniform motion.
  2. If it was of the form $$y = y_0 + vt + \frac{1}{2}at^2$$, where $$a$$ would represent acceleration, it would indicate uniformly accelerated motion. The presence of the $$8t^2$$ term here plays a similar role, indicating that the motion is uniformly accelerated in the $$y$$-direction due to the constant acceleration implied by this term.

Since the motion in the $$y$$ direction is determined by a quadratic equation, and the path of the particle depends on both the $$x$$ and $$y$$ coordinates, the motion of the particle is not along a straight line but rather follows a parabolic path due to the quadratic (second-degree) dependence on time in the $$y$$-coordinate.

Additionally, the acceleration is not changing with time, as deduced from the constant coefficient of the $$t^2$$ term in the $$y$$ equation, indicating uniform acceleration. Therefore, the motion is uniformly accelerated and follows a parabolic path.

Hence, the correct answer is:

Option D: uniformly accelerated having motion along a parabolic path.

Motion in a Plane.question: The angle of projection for a projectile to have same horizontal range and maximum height is :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
To find the angle of projection for a projectile to have the same horizontal range and maximum height, we need to express both the range and the maximum height in terms of the projectile's initial velocity and the angle of projection, and then set them equal to each other.

The formula for the horizontal range $R$ of a projectile is given by:

$R = \frac{v^2}{g} \sin 2\theta,$

where $v$ is the initial velocity of the projectile, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, and $\theta$ is the angle of projection.

The formula for the maximum height $H$ reached by the projectile is:

$H = \frac{v^2}{2g} \sin^2\theta.$

To have the same numerical value for $R$ and $H$, we set them equal to each other:

$\frac{v^2}{g} \sin 2\theta = \frac{v^2}{2g} \sin^2\theta.$

Simplifying this equation, we get:

$2 \sin 2\theta = \sin^2\theta.$

Using the double-angle formula, $\sin 2\theta = 2 \sin\theta \cos\theta$, we can rewrite the equation as:

$4 \sin\theta \cos\theta = \sin^2\theta.$

This can be simplified further to:

$4 \sin\theta \cos\theta = (\sin\theta)^2.$

Dividing both sides by $\sin\theta$ (assuming $\sin\theta \neq 0$), we get:

$4 \cos\theta = \sin\theta.$

Now, dividing both sides by $\cos\theta$, we have:

$4 = \tan\theta.$

So, the angle of projection $\theta$ is:

$\theta = \tan^{-1}(4).$

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option D $$\tan ^{-1}(4)$$.

y = a sin$$\omega $$t and

The speed of the particle is :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
Given that,

x = a cos $$\omega $$t

y = a sin $$\omega $$t

z = a $$\omega $$t

Velocity in x-direction,

Vx = $${{dx} \over {dt}} = - a\omega \sin \omega t$$

Velocity in y-direction,

Vy = $${{dy} \over {dt}}$$ = a $$\omega $$cos $$\omega $$t

Velocity in z-direction,

Vz = $${{dz} \over {dt}}$$ = a$$\omega $$

Net velocity,

$$\overrightarrow V $$ = Vx$$\widehat i$$ + Vy$$\widehat j$$ + Vz$$\widehat k$$

Speed = $$\left| {\overrightarrow V } \right| = \sqrt {V_x^2 + V_y^2 + V_z^2} $$

$$ = \sqrt {{a^2}{\omega ^2}{{\sin }^2}\omega t + {a^2}{\omega ^2}{{\cos }^2}\omega t + {a^2}{\omega ^2}} $$

$$ = \sqrt {2{a^2}{\omega ^2}} $$

$$ = \sqrt 2 a\omega $$

east and $$\mathop j\limits^ \wedge  $$ , north. Ship B is at a distance of
80 km east and 150 km north of Ship A and
is sailing towards west at 10 km/hr. A will be
at minimum distance from B in :

Time after which the distance is minimum between A and B can be calculated as

$$ = {{3200 + 7500} \over {4100}} = {{10700} \over {4100}} = 2.6$$ h

Motion in a Plane.question: Position of an ant ($$\mathrm{S}$$ in metres) moving in $$\mathrm{Y}$$-$$\mathrm{Z}$$ plane is given by $$S=2 t^2 \hat{j}+5 \hat{k}$$ (where $$t$$ is in second). The magnitude and direction of velocity of the ant at $$\mathrm{t}=1 \mathrm{~s}$$ will be :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
The position of an ant, denoted as $ \mathrm{S} $ in meters, moving in the $ \mathrm{Y} $-$ \mathrm{Z} $ plane is given by $ S = 2t^2 \hat{j} + 5 \hat{k} $, where $ t $ is in seconds. To determine the magnitude and direction of the ant's velocity at $ t = 1 $ second, we need to differentiate the position function with respect to time.

The velocity $ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} $ is given by:

$$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} = \frac{d\mathrm{S}}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt} (2t^2 \hat{j} + 5 \hat{k})$$

On differentiating, we get:

$$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} = 4t \hat{j}$$

At $ t = 1 $ second:

$$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} = 4 \cdot 1 \hat{j} = 4 \hat{j}$$

Therefore, the magnitude of the velocity is $ 4 \mathrm{~m/s} $ and it is directed along the $ y $-axis.

Motion in a Plane.question: Let $$\overrightarrow A $$ = $$\left( {\widehat i + \widehat j} \right)$$ and, $$\overrightarrow B  = \left( {2\widehat i - \widehat j} \right).$$ The magnitude of a coplanar vector $$\overrightarrow C $$ such that $$\overrightarrow A .\overrightarrow C  = \overrightarrow B .\overrightarrow C  = \overrightarrow A .\overrightarrow B ,$$ is given by :

value of $$\left( {2\mathop {{A_1}}\limits^ \to   + 3\mathop {{A_2}}\limits^ \to  } \right)\left( {3\mathop {{A_1}}\limits^ \to   - \mathop {2{A_2}}\limits^ \to  } \right)$$

Motion in a Plane.question: If $$\overrightarrow A $$ and $$\overrightarrow B $$ are two vectors satisfying the relation $$\overrightarrow A $$ . $$\overrightarrow B $$ = $$\left| {\overrightarrow A  \times \overrightarrow B } \right|$$. Then the value of $$\left| {\overrightarrow A  - \overrightarrow B } \right|$$ will be :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
Given, $$\overrightarrow A $$ . $$\overrightarrow B $$ = $$\left| {\overrightarrow A \times \overrightarrow B } \right|$$ ..... (i)

Also, we know that

$$\overrightarrow A $$ . $$\overrightarrow B $$ = $$\left| {\overrightarrow A } \right|\left| {\overrightarrow B } \right|$$ cos$$\theta$$ .... (ii)

and $$\overrightarrow A \times \overrightarrow B $$ = $$\left| {\overrightarrow A } \right|\left| {\overrightarrow B } \right|$$ sin$$\theta$$ ..... (iii)

From Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get

$$\left| {\overrightarrow A } \right|\left| {\overrightarrow B } \right|$$ cos$$\theta$$ = $$\left| {\overrightarrow A } \right|\left| {\overrightarrow B } \right|$$ sin$$\theta$$

$$ \Rightarrow \cos \theta = \sin \theta \Rightarrow {{\sin \theta } \over {\cos \theta }} = 1$$

$$ \Rightarrow \tan \theta = 1$$

$$ \Rightarrow \tan \theta = \tan 45^\circ \Rightarrow \theta = 45^\circ $$

$$\therefore$$ $$\left| {\overrightarrow A - \overrightarrow B } \right| = \sqrt {{A^2} + {B^2} - 2\left| {\overrightarrow A } \right|\left| {\overrightarrow B } \right|\cos \theta } $$

$$ = \sqrt {{A^2} + {B^2} - 2\left| {\overrightarrow A } \right|\left| {\overrightarrow B } \right|\cos (45^\circ )} $$

$$ = \sqrt {{A^2} + {B^2} - \sqrt 2 AB} $$

$$ = 0$$

The angle between $${\overrightarrow A }$$ and $${\overrightarrow B }$$ is -

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,n\left( {2a\cos {\theta \over 2}} \right) = 2a{{\sin \theta } \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,\tan {\theta \over 2} = n$$

Motion in a Plane.question: Two vectors $${\overrightarrow P }$$ and $${\overrightarrow Q }$$ have equal magnitudes. If the magnitude of $${\overrightarrow P  + \overrightarrow Q }$$ is n times the magnitude of $${\overrightarrow P  - \overrightarrow Q }$$, then angle between $${\overrightarrow P }$$ and $${\overrightarrow Q }$$ is :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$$\left| {\overrightarrow P } \right| = \left| {\overrightarrow Q } \right| = x$$ ..... (i)

$$\left| {\overrightarrow P + \overrightarrow Q } \right| = n\left| {\overrightarrow P - \overrightarrow Q } \right|$$

$${P^2} + {Q^2} + 2PQ\cos \theta = {n^2}({P^2} + {Q^2} - 2PQ\cos \theta )$$

Using (i) in above equation

$$\cos \theta = {{{n^2} - 1} \over {1 + {n^2}}}$$

$$\theta = {\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{{n^2} - 1} \over {{n^2} + 1}}} \right)$$

Motion in a Plane.question: Two vectors $$\overrightarrow X $$ and $$\overrightarrow Y $$ have equal magnitude. The magnitude of ($$\overrightarrow X $$ $$-$$ $$\overrightarrow Y $$) is n times the magnitude of ($$\overrightarrow X $$ + $$\overrightarrow Y $$). The angle between $$\overrightarrow X $$ and $$\overrightarrow Y $$ is :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
Given X = Y

$$\sqrt {{X^2} + {Y^2} - 2 \times Y\cos \theta } $$

$$ = n\sqrt {{X^2} + {Y^2} + 2 \times Y\cos \theta } $$

Square both sides

$$2{X^2}(1 - \cos \theta ) = {n^2}.2{X^2}(1 + \cos \theta )$$

$$1 - \cos \theta = {n^2} + {n^2}\cos \theta $$

$$\cos \theta = {{1 - {n^2}} \over {1 + {n^2}}}$$

$$\theta = {\cos ^{ - 1}}\left[ {{{{n^2} - 1} \over { - {n^2} - 1}}} \right]$$

Motion in a Plane.question: Two vectors $$\overrightarrow A $$ and $$\overrightarrow B $$ have equal magnitudes. If magnitude of $$\overrightarrow A $$ + $$\overrightarrow B $$ is equal to two times the magnitude of $$\overrightarrow A $$ $$-$$ $$\overrightarrow B $$, then the angle between $$\overrightarrow A $$ and $$\overrightarrow B $$ will be :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$$\sqrt {{A^2} + {A^2} + 2{A^2}\cos \theta } = 2\sqrt {{A^2} + {A^2} + 2{A^2}( - \cos \theta )} $$

$$ \Rightarrow 2{A^2} + 2{A^2}\cos \theta = 8{A^2} + 8{A^2} - ( - \cos \theta )$$

$$ \Rightarrow 5\cos \theta = 3$$

$$ \Rightarrow \theta = {\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( {{3 \over 5}} \right)$$

Motion in a Plane.question: If two vectors $$\vec{A}$$ and $$\vec{B}$$ having equal magnitude $$R$$ are inclined at angle $$\theta$$, then
Motion in a Plane.solution:
The magnitude of resultant vector

$$R^{\prime}=\sqrt{a^2+b^2+2 a b \cos \theta}$$

Here $$a=b=R$$

Then $$R^{\prime}=\sqrt{R^2+R^2+2 R^2 \cos \theta}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & =R \sqrt{2} \sqrt{1+\cos \theta} \\ & =\sqrt{2} R \sqrt{2 \cos ^2 \frac{\theta}{2}} \\ & =2 R \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Motion in a Plane.question: The angle between vector $$\vec{Q}$$ and the resultant of $$(2 \vec{Q}+2 \vec{P})$$ and $$(2 \vec{Q}-2 \vec{P})$$ is :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
To find the angle between the vector $$\vec{Q}$$ and the resultant of $$(2 \vec{Q}+2 \vec{P})$$ and $$(2 \vec{Q}-2 \vec{P})$$, we first find the resultant vector of $$(2 \vec{Q}+2 \vec{P})$$ and $$(2 \vec{Q}-2 \vec{P})$$.

The resultant vector of $$(2 \vec{Q}+2 \vec{P})$$ and $$(2 \vec{Q}-2 \vec{P})$$ can be simply found by adding these two vectors:

$$ \text{Resultant} = (2 \vec{Q}+2 \vec{P}) + (2 \vec{Q}-2 \vec{P}) = 4 \vec{Q} $$

Now, we need to find the angle between the vector $$\vec{Q}$$ and this resultant vector $$4\vec{Q}$$. Since the resultant vector is just a scaled version of $$\vec{Q}$$, they are in the same direction. The angle between any vector and another vector that is a scaled version of the first vector is always $$0^\circ$$, because they are parallel to each other.

Therefore, the angle between $$\vec{Q}$$ and the resultant of $$(2 \vec{Q}+2 \vec{P})$$ and $$(2 \vec{Q}-2 \vec{P})$$ is $$0^\circ$$.

So, the correct option is:

Option B: $$0^\circ$$

Motion in a Plane.solution:
Projection = $${{\overrightarrow A .\overrightarrow B } \over {\left| {\overrightarrow B } \right|}}(\widehat B)$$

$$ = {{(\widehat i + \widehat j + \widehat k).(\widehat i + \widehat j)} \over {\sqrt 2 }}{{(\widehat i + \widehat j)} \over {\sqrt 2 }}$$

$$ = {2 \over {\sqrt 2 }} $$$$ \times $$$$ {{(\widehat i + \widehat j)} \over {\sqrt 2 }}$$

$$ = (\widehat i + \widehat j)$$

Motion in a Plane.question: A vector in $x-y$ plane makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with $y$-axis. The magnitude of $\mathrm{y}$-component of vector is $2 \sqrt{3}$. The magnitude of $x$-component of the vector will be :
Motion in a Plane.solution:
$$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{A} \cos 30^{\circ}=2 \sqrt{3} \\\\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{A} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=2 \sqrt{3} \\\\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{A}=4 \end{aligned} $$

Now $A_x=A \sin 30^{\circ}=4 \times \frac{1}{2}=2$
```
